summary: This experimental document proposes raising TCP's permitted initial window from between 2 and 4 segments to 10 segments, falling back to the older recommendation if problems appear. It explains the motivation, weighs the pros and cons, and reports large-scale experiments in which the larger window improved performance for many web services.

eli5.summary: When two computers start talking, TCP lets only a few packets go out first. This tries letting more go at once so pages load faster, backing off if the road gets crowded.

subtitle: Why TCP's first burst of data was allowed to grow from 2 to 4 segments up to 10, and what to watch for when doing it.

tldr.problem: A new TCP connection may send only 2 to 4 segments before hearing back, which wastes round trips on the short transfers that dominate web traffic.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC raises the upper bound on the initial window to 10 segments, with a cap of 14600 bytes, and asks anyone enabling it to monitor results and fall back to the RFC 3390 value if problems appear.
tldr.outcome: This is an Experimental RFC. Google's large-scale tests showed lower latency with a small rise in retransmissions, but it asks for more experiments before a larger window is on by default.

today: RFC 6928 is an Experimental RFC and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text itself says a follow-up document might revisit whether a larger initial window can be used by default, and that tighter specifications could lead to a future Standards Track document.

sections.title: The Proposal in Brief
sections.content:
RFC 6928 proposes to raise the upper bound on TCP's initial window (IW) to 10 segments, with a maximum of 14600 bytes. It is patterned after RFC 3390, which allowed between 2 and 4 segments. Some recommendations are conditional on extra monitoring because of lingering concerns about other flows sharing the same bottleneck.

The main argument is that the Internet has grown. The RFC says ten segments are likely to fit into the queue space at any broadband access link, even with a reasonable number of concurrent connections. Slower links can use environment-specific settings instead.

The document recommends that all TCP implementations have a settable IW parameter, as long as there is a reasonable effort to monitor for side effects. It also makes a minor revision to RFC 3390 and RFC 5681 so the window is not reset when a SYN or SYN/ACK is lost.
sections.eli5: TCP starts each conversation by sending only a few packets. This RFC says the first batch can safely be bigger, but people should keep watching to make sure nothing breaks.

sections.title: The Modified Initial Window Rule
sections.content:
The upper bound for the initial window becomes min (10*MSS, max (2*MSS, 14600)). Using a larger window is optional: a TCP MAY still start with fewer than 10 segments. The change covers the first round-trip time of data during or after the three-way handshake, and neither the SYN/ACK nor its ACK should increase the window.

RFC 3390 required one segment after a lost SYN or SYN/ACK. Because the default retransmission timeout was being reduced to 1 second (RFC 6298), that could penalize connections with a round-trip time over 1 second. The RFC therefore RECOMMENDS not resetting to 1 segment unless there have been more than one SYN or SYN/ACK retransmissions or true loss detection has been made.

Slow start is used for the initial window, the restart window after idle time, and the loss window after a retransmit timeout. This RFC changes only the initial window. The loss window must remain 1 segment. Implementations SHOULD fall back to RFC 3390 for the restart window if loss is detected in the initial or a restart window and more than 4 KB was sent.
sections.eli5: There is a simple formula for how many packets can go out first, and the answer is at most 10. If something goes wrong after a restart, the sender goes back to the smaller, safer amount.

sections.title: Why a Bigger Window Helps
sections.content:
Today's traffic is dominated by short web connections, and the RFC argues the small initial window has become a limit on web performance. The window had stayed at 4 KB for a decade. Browsers have worked around it by opening several connections to the same site, up to six per domain at the time, which works against congestion control. The authors hope a modest increase will help stop that trend.

Going from 3 to 10 segments reduces total transfer time for data sets larger than 4 KB by up to 4 round trips. For example, a transfer of 32 segments needs 2 rather than 5 round trips. Web objects have also grown, so only a small share fit in a 4 KB window. A larger window also gives fast retransmit, which needs three duplicate ACKs, a better chance to repair loss without waiting for a timeout.

The round-trip table assumes infinite bandwidth, no packet loss, and standard delayed ACKs.
sections.eli5: If you can carry only three books per trip, a big pile takes many trips. Carrying ten at a time means far fewer trips, so everything arrives sooner.

sections.title: Risks and Mitigations
sections.content:
Bigger bursts can overflow small router buffers and cause drops, which may lead to unnecessary retransmit timeouts. The RFC notes that most access routers buffer enough for 130 ms or longer, enough for more than 10 packets at 1 Mbps, but possibly not enough when browsers open many connections at once. Because the increase happens only at the start of a connection, the RFC considers it unlikely to cause persistent congestion or congestion collapse, although that may not hold if applications open many simultaneous connections.

Until the change is widely deployed, flows using the larger window could be unfair to flows following RFC 3390, though no severe unfairness was found. Large queues at access networks (bufferbloat) could also be made worse by short downloads. Hosts on slow links can advertise an initial receive window smaller than 10 segments. Implementations MUST follow RFC 6298 and restart the retransmission timer on each ACK for new data, to limit spurious timeouts.
sections.eli5: A big first scoop can overflow a small bucket on a slow road. So computers on slow roads can ask for smaller scoops, and everyone keeps an eye out for jams.

sections.title: Large-Scale Test Results
sections.content:
The RFC summarizes experiments on Google's front-end infrastructure in two data centers. In AvgDC (median connection speed about 1.7 Mbps), average web search latency improved by 11.7% (68 ms). In SlowDC, which has more slow subnets, it improved by 8.7% (72 ms). Gains were largest, over 20%, on high round-trip-time and high bandwidth-delay-product networks, and about 5% on low round-trip-time paths. Low-bandwidth subnets saw 10 to 20% improvements.

The cost was a modest rise in retransmissions: from 1.98% to 2.29% in AvgDC and from 3.54% to 4.21% in SlowDC. The Maps application, which uses multiple concurrent connections, rose from 3.94% to 5.79% in SlowDC, and its 99th percentile latency there rose by 2.3% (80 ms). The authors conjecture that buffering at bottleneck links plays a key role. Appendix A also records that 10 segments seemed to give most of the benefit without a significant rise in retransmissions, and that SACK was not required for IW=10 to beat IW=3.
sections.eli5: When they tried it for real, pages loaded faster for most people. A few more packets had to be sent again, but the speedup was worth it.

sections.title: Deployment Guidance
sections.content:
The RFC says further experiments are needed before a larger initial window is enabled by default in the Internet. Anyone turning it on SHOULD monitor performance before and after, watching the rate of packet losses, ECN marking, and segment retransmissions during the initial burst. A sender SHOULD cache information about connections that used a larger window, and new connections SHOULD fall back to the RFC 3390 window if there is evidence of problems.

An increased initial window MUST NOT be turned on by default on systems without monitoring capabilities. Users who see significant deterioration SHOULD fall back to the RFC 3390 window. The RFC also notes there were no adequate studies of the impact on real-time traffic such as VoIP. Its security section says the change raises no known new security issues, since it is highly unlikely to cause persistent congestion.
sections.eli5: Turn the bigger scoop on carefully. Keep a close eye on how things go, and go back to the smaller scoop if people start having trouble.
